claim: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) comprises up to ~10–20% of all breast cancer cases.
source: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) comprises up to ~10–20% of all cases.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the prevalence of TNBC supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: TNBC tumors are clinically aggressive, usually with larger sizes at initial presentation, of high pathological grade, and likely to have lymph node involvement and early recurrence in visceral sites.
source: These heterogeneous tumors are clinically aggressive, usually with larger sizes at initial presentation, of high pathological grade, and likely to have lymph node involvement and early recurrence in visceral sites (Dietze et al., 2015; Newman and Kaljee, 2017; Schettini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Despite optimal management, many TNBC patients have distant metastases and poor disease outcomes.
source: Despite optimal management, many patients have distant metastases and poor disease outcomes (Biswas et al., 2016; Coughlin, 2019; Dent et al., 2007; Perou et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Checkpoint inhibitors and PARP inhibitors have recently been approved for TNBC in certain settings.
source: Combination chemotherapy has long been the standard therapeutic option but checkpoint inhibitors and poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors have recently been approved in certain settings (Garrido-Castro et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019; Lyons and Traina, 2019; Marra et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: A biological hallmark of TNBC is an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that fosters tumor growth and metastatic spread.
source: A biological hallmark of TNBC is an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that fosters tumor growth and metastatic spread through the suppression of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and secretion of immunoinhibitory cytokines, mainly by tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) (DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; Lim et al., 2018; Wagner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TAM are classically divided into M1 and M2 populations, with M1 associated with antitumor activity and M2 with tumor progression.
source: TAM are classically divided into two major populations, M1 and M2, representing the extremes of a broad activation state spectrum; the M1 population is associated with antitumor activity while the M2 population with tumor progression (DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; Lim et al., 2018; Wagner et al., 2019; Biswas and Mantovani, 2010; Tan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: EF43.fgf4 cells do not express the estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, or Erbb2/Neu.
source: The EF43.fgf4 syngeneic mouse mammary gland tumor (Adams et al., 1987; Hajitou et al., 1998) is highly infiltrated by TAM and also serves as an immunocompetent TNBC model since EF43.fgf4 cells do not express the estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, or Erbb2/Neu (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing immunoblotting analysis.

claim: After three rounds of in vivo phage display selection, the pool of tumor-homing phage showed an ~300 fold enrichment relative to normal tissues.
source: After the third round, the pool of tumor-homing phage showed an ~300 fold enrichment relative to normal tissues (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The dominant peptide CSSTRESAC was more strongly enriched (16-fold) than each of the other three peptides.
source: Notably, the dominant peptide CSSTRESAC was more strongly enriched (16-fold) than each of the other three peptides (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The peptide CSSTRESAC did not bind to EF43.fgf4 cells in vitro.
source: With a standard cell binding assay (Giordano et al., 2001), we found that the peptides CRGFVVGRC, CQRALMIAC, and CRYSAARSC bound to EF43.fgf4 cells, whereas the peptide CSSTRESAC did not (Figure 1B), indicating that CSSTRESAC might indeed recognize non-malignant stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell binding assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CSSTRESAC-phage particles bound specifically to CD11b+F4/80+ macrophages isolated from tumors.
source: Binding assays to each of these cell subpopulations showed that CSSTRESAC-phage particles bound specifically to CD11b+F4/80+ macrophage; binding to tumor-isolated EF43.fgf4 cells and CD45R+ cells were at background levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The macrophage population (CD11b+F4/80+) constituted a large portion of the non-malignant cellular component of EF43.fgf4-derived mammary tumors.
source: Similar to human breast cancers known to be highly infiltrated by macrophages (Biswas et al., 2016; Dent et al., 2007; Perou et al., 2000; Garrido-Castro et al., 2019; Khan et al., 2019; Marra et al., 2019; DeNardo and Ruffell, 2019; Lim et al., 2018; Wagner et al., 2019; Biswas and Mantovani, 2010; Tan et al., 2019; Adams et al., 1987; Hajitou et al., 1998; Giordano et al., 2001), the macrophage population (CD11b+F4/80+) constituted a large portion of the non-malignant cellular component of EF43.fgf4-derived mammary tumors, followed by a lesser population of B lymphocytes (CD45R+).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and flow cytometry data.

claim: T-lymphocytes (CD8+ or CD4+) were not detected in EF43.fgf4 tumors.
source: T-lymphocytes (CD8+ or CD4+) were not detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Binding of the CSSTRESAC-phage to MMTV-PyMT tumors was higher compared to a control organ (~3-fold) or to a negative control phage (~2.5-fold).
source: Binding of the CSSTRESAC-phage to MMTV-PyMT tumors was higher compared to a control organ (~3-fold) or to a negative control phage (~2.5-fold) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: CSSTRESAC-targeted liposomes showed increased contrast enhancement in MDA-MB-231 breast tumor xenografts after 3 hr of systemic circulation and persisted through 24 and 48 hr.
source: An increased contrast enhancement in breast tumor xenografts receiving CSSTRESAC-targeted liposomes was clearly detected after 3 hr of systemic circulation and persisted through 24 and 48 hr (B-C) compared to control liposomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: Immunoblotting of eluted fractions revealed the presence of two vitamin D-binding receptor candidates: PDIA3 and DBP.
source: Notably, immunoblotting of eluted fractions revealed the presence of two vitamin D-binding receptor candidates: protein disulfide-isomerase A3 (PDIA3; also known as glucose-regulated protein-58 kDa, GRP58; endoplasmic reticulum protein of 57 kDa, ERp57; and membrane-associated rapid response to steroid-binding, 1,25D3-MARRS) (Khanal and Nemere, 2007; Figure 1E, top panel) and vitamin D-binding protein (DBP) (Figure 1E, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1E and citation.

claim: In vitro binding assays to recombinant PDIA3 and DBP confirmed preferential binding of CSSTRESAC-phage relative to the negative control insertless phage.
source: In vitro binding assays to recombinant PDIA3 and DBP confirmed preferential binding of CSSTRESAC-phage relative to the negative control insertless phage (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PDIA3 and DBP both bind to vitamin D.
source: PDIA3 and DBP both bind to vitamin D (Christakos et al., 2016), thereby suggesting that CSSTRESAC might be structurally similar to vitamin D.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Experimental binding of CSSTRESAC-phage to immobilized DBP was reduced by increasing amounts of 1,25-(OH)2D3 but not by the non-active precursor vitamin D3.
source: Indeed, experimental binding of CSSTRESAC-phage to immobilized DBP was reduced (Student's t-test, p<0.05) by increasing amounts of 1,25-(OH)2D3 but not by the non-active precursor vitamin D3 (Figure 1K), a biochemical finding consistent with the computational model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental binding data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis showed robust expression of PDIA3 on the surface of CD11b+IL-10highIL-12low TAM.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed robust expression of PDIA3 on the surface of CD11b+IL-10highIL-12low TAM (Figure 2A), identifying PDIA3 as a new cell membrane-associated candidate marker of M2-polarized macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EF43.fgf4 cells isolated from tumors did not express PDIA3.
source: Consistently, EF43.fgf4 cells isolated from tumors did not express PDIA3 (Figure 2B), in agreement with the lack of CSSTRESAC-phage binding to EF43.fgf4 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining of frozen breast tumor sections suggested co-localization between PDIA3 and CD68.
source: Moreover, immunofluorescence staining of frozen breast tumor sections from tumor-bearing mice receiving CSSTRESAC-phage iv suggested co-localization between PDIA3 and CD68, a well-established cell surface marker of macrophages (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Administration of an anti-PDIA3 antibody into EF43.fgf4 tumor-bearing mice confirmed accessibility of PDIA3 through the systemic circulation.
source: Finally, administration of an anti-PDIA3 antibody into EF43.fgf4 tumor-bearing mice confirmed accessibility of PDIA3 through the systemic circulation (Ozawa et al., 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and a citation.

claim: Treatment of CD11b+F4/80+ TAM with the soluble CSSTRESAC peptide induced a marked (~40 fold) increase in gene expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6.
source: Treatment of CD11b+F4/80+ TAM with the soluble CSSTRESAC peptide induced a marked (on average ~40 fold) increase in gene expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The cellular response to CSSTRESAC was abrogated when CSSTRESA-treated CD11b+F4/80+ TAM were co-treated with 1,25-(OH)2D3.
source: This cellular response was abrogated when CSSTRESA-treated CD11b+F4/80+ TAM were co-treated with 1,25-(OH)2D3 (Figure 2F,G), verifying that it was specifically caused by the binding of the CSSTRESAC peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: A significant delay in tumor growth of mice treated with CSSTRESAC was observed as soon as one-week post initiation of treatment, compared to tumors of mice receiving an unrelated control peptide or vehicle alone.
source: A significant delay in tumor growth of mice treated with CSSTRESAC was observed as soon as one-week post initiation of treatment, compared to tumors of mice receiving an unrelated control peptide or vehicle alone (Figure 3A, t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: FACS analysis showed a reduction in the number of CD11b+IL10highIL12lowPDIA3-expressing TAM in tumors from mice treated with soluble CSSTRESAC peptide.
source: FACS analysis of CD11b+F4/80+ TAM showed a reduction in the number of CD11b+IL10highIL12lowPDIA3-expressing TAM in tumors from mice treated with soluble CSSTRESAC peptide as compared to the negative control groups (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By the end of the experiment, the sizes of tumors in mice that received CSSTRESAC-AAVP-HSVtk were significantly smaller than that of mice receiving control fd-AAVP-HSVtk or vehicle alone.
source: By the end of the experiment, the sizes of tumors in mice that received CSSTRESAC-AAVP-HSVtk were significantly smaller than that of mice receiving control fd-AAVP-HSVtk or vehicle alone (Figure 3C, t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor size data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: Macrophage quantification showed a reduction in the number of F480+CD11b+IL10highIL12lowPDIA3-expressing TAM after CSSTRESAC-AAVP-HSVtk treatment.
source: Moreover, macrophage quantification showed a reduction in the number of F480+CD11b+IL10highIL12lowPDIA3-expressing TAM (Figure 3D) accompanied by a shift in the cytokine profile toward an inflammatory response in the tumor microenvironment (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mathematical model predicted that infusion of CCSTRESAC would result in ~400 mm3 greater reduction in tumor volume compared to bolus.
source: Our mathematical model predicted that infusion of CCSTRESAC would result in ~400 mm3 greater reduction in tumor volume compared to bolus (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling predictions shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An unsupervised clustering analysis showed that high levels of PDIA3 expression in TAM clustered positively with markers of M2-polarized TAM as well as poor prognosis indicators and genes associated with immune suppression.
source: An unsupervised clustering analysis (Figure 5) showed that high levels of PDIA3 expression in TAM clustered positively with markers of M2-polarized TAM as well as poor prognosis indicators and genes associated with immune suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PDIA3 is a functional receptor expressed on the cell surface of the M2-like class of TAM in TNBC.
source: We report that PDIA3 is a functional receptor expressed on the cell surface of the M2-like class of TAM in TNBC.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: PDIA3 has immunoregulatory functions as the TAM cell surface receptor for the peptide CSSTRESAC.
source: We show that PDIA3, an established vitamin D-interacting protein, has immunoregulatory functions as the TAM cell surface receptor for the peptide CSSTRESAC, with clear effects in preclinical non-TNBC and TNBC mouse models and, at least potentially, in TNBC patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cytokine changes and tumor growth effects.

claim: TNBCs are more likely to respond to immunotherapy due to higher numbers of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, higher levels of PD-L1 expression, and a higher mutational burden.
source: In particular, TNBCs are more likely to respond to immunotherapy due to higher numbers of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, higher levels of PD-L1 expression in both tumor cells and immunce cells as well as a higher mutational burden and the consequent rise in tumor-specific neo-antigens.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about TNBC characteristics.

claim: The Human Protein Atlas shows cytoplasmic expression of PDIA3 in human breast cancer cells.
source: Notably, the Human Protein Atlas shows cytoplasmic expression of PDIA3 in human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Human Protein Atlas database.

claim: CSSTRESAC is rapidly cleared through renal excretion.
source: Therefore, the half-life of the CSSTRESAC conforms to those of other targeting pharmacological data (Pasqualini et al., 2015) and indicates that soluble CSSTRESAC is rapidly cleared through renal excretion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the calculated half-life and supported by citation to similar pharmacological data.

claim: Liposome uptake was low in all organs except the liver.
source: Liposome uptake was low in all organs except the liver, a well-known biological phenomenon due to the relatively large size and cationic charge of liposomes (targeted or control), and their non-specific uptake by the reticuloendothelial system.
evidence: This claim is supported by biodistribution data and established knowledge about liposome pharmacokinetics.

claim: None of the liposome preparations caused liver toxicity as confirmed by levels of ALT and AST measured in serum of treated mice.
source: None of the liposome preparations caused liver toxicity as confirmed by levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) measured in serum of treated mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by ALT and AST measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The computed model suggests that CSSTRESAC binds at a similar site on the surface of DBP as 1,25-(OH)2D3 and its metabolite calcidiol.
source: The outcome of the Rosetta FlexPepDock calculations suggests that although CSSTRESAC binds at a similar site on the surface of DBP as 1,25-(OH)2D3 and its metabolite calcidiol, it is unlikely to interact more tightly and should be competitively displaced by the natural ligands of the receptor protein (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: CSSTRESAC targets a range of different breast tumors independently of their ligand display context, tumor cell species, or host immunocompetency status.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that CSSTRESAC targets a range of different breast tumors (in xenograft, genetic, and syngeneic mouse models) independently of their ligand display context, tumor cell species, or host immunocompetency status.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple tumor models.

claim: Extracellular expression of PDIA3 was largely restricted to resident macrophage in tumors, while control tissues showed minimal cell surface staining.
source: Notably, extracellular expression of PDIA3 was largely restricted to resident macrophage in tumors, while control tissues showed minimal cell surface staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and antibody administration experiments.

claim: Treatment of tumors with the soluble CSSTRESAC peptide inhibited tumor growth and altered the TAM population in tumors.
source: Thus, treatment of tumors with the soluble CSSTRESAC peptide inhibited tumor growth and altered the TAM population in tumors, which supports it as a potential antitumor drug lead candidate.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth and FACS analysis data.

claim: The CSSTRESAC-DBP complex specifically binds to PDIA3 and elicits functional changes in PDIA3-expressing TAM within the tumor microenvironment.
source: Our proposed working hypothesis shows that the CSSTRESAC-DBP complex specifically binds to PDIA3 and elicits functional changes in PDIA3-expressing TAM within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This is a working hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Biochemical and cellular alterations caused by CSSTRESAC may result in an inflammatory local response potentially mediated by IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, and inhibition of tumor growth.
source: Such biochemical and cellular alterations may in turn result in an inflammatory local response potentially mediated by IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α, and inhibition of tumor growth (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cytokine expression data and tumor growth results.

claim: The mathematical model shows that native competing serum 1,25-(OH)2D3 is unlikely to influence the binding of CSSTRESAC to its target on TAM.
source: Finally, one should note that our mathematical model shows that native competing serum 1,25-(OH)2D3 is unlikely to influence the binding of CSSTRESAC to its target on TAM.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling predictions.

claim: CSSTRESAC could be considered as a new non-steroidal vitamin D analogue prototype for drug lead-optimization.
source: In this setting, CSSTRESAC could also be considered as a new non-steroidal vitamin D analogue prototype for drug lead-optimization, with applications that may include other diseases (malignant or non-malignant) with an inflammatory component.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications based on the findings.

claim: Combination therapy with immunomodulators may increase the therapeutic response against highly inflammatory tumors when combined with CSSTRESAC.
source: The effects of soluble CSSTRESAC and CSSTRESAC-AAVP-HSVtk in the local and systemic immune responses in murine models of breast cancer also suggest that combination therapy with immunomodulators may increase the therapeutic response against highly inflammatory tumors.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed effects in mouse models.

claim: CSSTRESAC-mediated immunoregulatory functions might become a medically meaningful translational strategy in breast cancer and other TAM-infiltrated cancers.
source: Therefore, immunomodulation of the local and/or systemic responses with immune checkpoint inhibitors could—at least in theory—be amplified by CSSTRESAC-mediated immunoregulatory functions in breast cancer, as well as other TAM-infiltrated cancers, and might perhaps become a medically meaningful translational strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical applications.

claim: Drug interactions caused by prolonged exposure to CSSTRESAC in the presence of steroids might confound the investigational use of CSSTRESAC-based therapies.
source: Similarly, drug interactions caused by prolonged exposure to CSSTRESAC in the presence of steroids—which are often used in cancer patients—might confound the investigational use of CSSTRESAC-based therapies and should be carefully considered.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential drug interactions.
